data.title: A high affinity and specificity anti-HER2 single-domain antibody (VHH) that targets trastuzumab's epitope with versatile biochemical, biological, and medical applications
data.abstract: In the past decade, various single-domain antibodies from llamas, also known as VHH or nanobody, have been discovered with applications in tumor imaging and cancer therapy. However, the potential application of anti-HER2 VHHs as a diagnostic tool suitable for ELISA, flow cytometry, cell imaging, bispecific antibody engineering, and immunohistochemistry has not been fully elucidated. To investigate this potential, HER2 antigen was expressed in HEK293 F cells, purified, and used to immunize llama. Using phage display, anti-HER2 VHHs with high affinity and specificity were isolated, sequenced, and constructed with a Histag and c-Myc tag. The constructed anti-HER2 VHHs were then expressed in E. coli, purified, and evaluated for their use in ELISA, flow cytometry, cell imaging, and immunohistochemistry. The affinities of the anti-HER2 VHHs toward the HER2 antigen were determined using biolayer interferometry. Furthermore, the binding sites of the anti-HER2 VHHs were evaluated by epitope mapping and in silico modeling and docking. Here, we report the sequence of an anti-HER2 VHH with high affinity (sub-nanomolar), specificity, and selectivity. This VHH binds to the same epitope as trastuzumab and can be utilized to generate bispecific antibodies or used as a diagnostic tool to differentiate HER2+ from HER2- antigens on plates, cells, and tissues. This discovery has broad applications in biochemical, biological, and medical sciences.
data.fulltext:
## Introduction:

Human epidermal growth factor receptor-2 (HER2), a member of the epidermal growth factor receptor family, also known as ERBB-2, is highly expressed in breast, ovarian, colorectal, and a variety of other solid tumors . As a result, HER2 has become a suitable target not only for cancer therapy but also for cancer diagnosis and phenotyping. Herceptin® (trastuzumab) was the first monoclonal antibody (mAb) to receive FDA (Food and Drug Administration) approval for the treatment of breast cancer patients with HER2 overexpression . Despite the effectiveness of anti-HER2 mAbs like Herceptin® in cancer therapy, their use for diagnostic purposes is limited due to side effects such as cardiotoxicity . It has been demonstrated that the Fc region of monoclonal antibodies (mAbs) can be recognized by the CD16 receptors on the surface of natural killer cells and macrophages leading to their activation and unwanted toxicity to normal tissues expressing HER2 . In addition to side effects, mAbs are bulky molecules (Mw ~150 kDa), which hampers their uniform penetration and diffusion throughout tumor tissues. To overcome these limitations, engineered antibody fragments such as F(ab’)2 (~110 kDa) , Fab (~57 kDa) , scFv (~ 28 kDa) , nanobodies (~15 kDa) , and affibodies (~7 kDa) , which have smaller sizes and lack the Fc region, are being investigated as a replacement for mAbs.

Heavy-chain-only antibodies (HcAbs), lacking light chains, were first found in the blood of the camelidae family . Compared with the antigen-binding fragment of conventional mAbs, HcAbs recognize their cognate antigen via the single variable domain of the heavy chain. This single variable domain, known as VHH (variable domain of the heavy chain of a heavy chain-only antibody), or nanobody, has a small size (~15 kDa) and lacks the Fc region . In addition to lacking the Fc region, VHHs possess unique characteristics, including high target specificity, affinity in the (sub-) nanomolar range, high stability, and ease of production in both mammalian and E. coli cells. These characteristics allow them to outperform conventional antibodies for imaging and radiotherapeutic purposes. Moreover, due to their small sizes, VHHs have shorter half-life and can diffuse throughout the tumor tissues more easily than mAbs, resulting in lower toxicity and immunogenicity . Furthermore, VHHs are ideal candidates to detect hidden or cryptic epitopes in antigen cavities, the ones that are not detectable by conventional mAbs .

In last decade, a few anti-HER2 VHHs have been developed for applications in tumor imaging and therapy . Currently, there is one radio-labeled anti-HER2 VHH in Phase II clinical trials, serving as a PET/CT imaging diagnostic tool for breast cancer phenotyping , and another in Phase I clinical trials for breast cancer therapy . However, the application of anti-HER2 VHHs as common reagents for ELISA, flow cytometry, cell imaging, and immunohistochemistry has not been fully elucidated. Here, we report the discovery of a tagged high-affinity and specificity/selectivity anti-HER2 VHH that binds to the same antigen as trastuzumab, with broad application in biochemical, biological, and medical sciences.

## Materials and Methods

### Expression and purification of recombinant HER2 protein and immunization of llama

The gene encoding the extracellular domain of HER2 (UniProt ID P04626) was designed, synthesized, and cloned into the PiggyBac plasmid vector (eHER2bac) under the control of the EF-1α promoter by VectorBuilder (IL, USA). A secretory signal was designed at the N-terminal and 12xHisTag at the C-terminal of the protein sequence to facilitate secretion of the expressed protein into the culture media and purification by Ni-NTA chromatography (Qiagen, MD, USA), respectively. The recombinant HER2 protein was then expressed in FreeStyle™ 293-F Cell system (Gibco, NY, USA), and purified as described previously . The purified recombinant HER2 protein was sent to Capralogics Inc. (Gilbertville, MA) to immunize the llama using the previously-published method .

### Isolation of peripheral blood mononuclear cells, library generation and phage display

Total peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated using Ficoll (Histopaque®−1077) (Sigma-Aldrich, MA, USA) method . The total RNA was extracted from isolated PBMCs using RNeasy Mini Kit (Qiagen, MD, USA), and cDNA was synthesized by SuperScript™ IV First-Strand Synthesis System (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) using oligo-dT and Random Hexamer. The VHH cDNAs were amplified by nested PCR using Q5® High-Fidelity DNA Polymerase (NEB, MA, USA) and two sets of designed primers (Supplementary Table 1) and the standard amplification protocol (Supplementary Table 2). The PCR products were cloned into pMECS-GG phagemid (Kindly provided by Dr. S. Muyldermans, Belgium) using SapI restriction enzyme (NEB, MA, USA) and T4 DNA ligase (NEB, MA, USA) using golden gate cloning, as described previously . Recombinant phagemids were then transformed into ten vials of 50 μL competent TG1 bacteria (Lucigen, WI, USA) by an electroporator.

For phage display, we adapted a previously published method . In brief, four rounds of panning were carried out to reach a specific anti-HER2 VHH library. Each round was carried out as described previously . Then, 100 μl of HER2 (1 μg/ml) protein was used to coat a 96-well plate and incubated at 4°C overnight. The following day, bacteria was pelleted by centrifugation (10,000 × g, 20 min, 4°C). The supernatant was transferred into a sterile and pre-chilled 50 ml tube, then 10% PEG-NaCl was added and incubated at 4°C for 1–2 h. Afterward, phages were collected by centrifugation (3,000 × g, 20 min, at 4°C) and washed twice using DPBS. Then, ELISA plate was blocked using 2% skimmed milk buffer (VWR, PA, USA). Concurrently, recombinant phages were incubated with blocking buffer while shaking. Next, 100 μl of recombinant phage displaying VHH of interest was added to the HER2-coated plate and incubated for 1 h at RT while shaking at 700 rpm. After washing ten times using DPBS/0.1% Tween and ten times using DPBS, bound phages were collected enzymatically using 0.25% trypsin (MiliporeSigma, MA, USA). 10 μl of harvested phages were incubated with 100 μl TG1 bacteria, at exponential growth, for 1 h at 37°C. Finally, 100 μl of infected TG1 was transferred into 100 ml LB media containing 100 μg/ml carbenicillin and bacterial culture continued overnight.

### Periplasmic extract and evaluation of affinity and specificity by ELISA

After four rounds of phage display, 190 colonies were screened to find the clone with the highest affinity toward HER2. First, 1 ml of LB broth supplemented with 100 μg/ml carbenicillin was added to a Deep-Well 96-well plate (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA). The plate was covered by a ventilating adhesive plate seal (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) to minimize potential contamination and evaporation. Next, one colony was inoculated into each well and incubated at 37°C overnight. The next day, 10 μl of overnight culture was transferred into a new Deep-Well 96-well plate containing 1 ml of LB broth supplemented with 100 μg/ml carbenicillin and incubated at 37°C for 4 h. Afterwards, the protein expression was induced by adding 1 mM IPTG (Teknova, CA, USA) and the bacterial culture was grown overnight at 28°C. The next day, the plate was spun down at 10,000 ×g for 10 min at 4°C, and the supernatants were discarded. To prepare the periplasmic extract, pelleted bacteria underwent freeze-thaw cycle three times (30 min at −20°C followed by 10 min at RT). Then, 500 μl DPBS was added to each pellet and incubated at RT for 30 min while shaking. The cell debris were removed by centrifugation and 400 μl of supernatant was gently transferred into a new 96-well plate and stored at 4°C.

For determination of affinity and specificity by ELISA, 100 μl of 1μg/ml HER2 protein and three other members of Heregulin superfamily including HER1, HER3, and HER4 (Abcam, MA, USA) were used to coat Nunc MaxiSorp™ high protein-binding capacity 96-well ELISA plates (Invitrogen, MA, USA) and incubated overnight at 4°C. The next day, each well was washed three times with washing buffer (DPBS + 0.1% Tween 20) and then incubated with blocking buffer, 2% skimmed milk, for 2 h at RT to block the free binding sites. Next, blocking buffer was replaced with 100 μl of periplasmic extract from above and incubated for 1 h at RT while shaking at 700 rpm. Each well was washed six times with washing buffer (DPBS + 0.1% Tween 20) followed by addition of 100 μl HRP Anti-HA tag antibody (Abcam, MA, USA) (1:10000 dilution) and incubation for 1 h at RT while shaking at 700 rpm. Each well was washed again six times, followed by addition of 50 μl 1-Step™ Turbo TMB-ELISA substrate solution (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA) and incubated at RT for 15 min (without shaking and in the dark). The reaction was stopped by adding 50 μl of stop solution (0.1 mM sulfuric acid) and the plate was read at 450 nm using 630 nm as a reference (450/630 nm).

### Expression and purification of anti-HER2 VHHs

The DNA sequences encoding the selected anti-HER2 VHHs were codon optimized, synthesized, and cloned into pHEN6c plasmid (Kindly provided by Dr. S. Muyldermans, Belgium) by GeneWiz (NJ, USA). The recombinant pHEN6c plasmids harboring VHH sequences were transformed into WK6 E. coli (ATCC, VA, USA) using heat shock. A 750 ml Terrific Broth (TB) media (IBI Scientific, IA, USA) was supplemented with 0.1% D-Glucose (MiliporeSigma, MA, USA), 1 mM MgCl2 and 100 μg/ml carbenicillin. The media was then inoculated with 10 ml of WK6 bacterial culture and grown at 37°C. When the OD600 reached 0.5–0.8, the protein expression was induced by 0.5 mM IPTG. Protein expression continued at 28°C overnight while shaking at 180 rpm. The next day, the bacterial culture was centrifuged (10,000 × g, 10 min, 4°C) to pellet the bacteria. The pellet was resuspended in 10 ml of TES buffer (200 mM Tris–HCl, pH 8.0, 500 mM sucrose, 1 mM EDTA) and incubated on ice for 1h while shaking. Then, 15 ml of TES buffer was diluted with distilled water to a total volume of 60 ml, added to the cell suspension, and incubated on ice for additional 45 min while shaking. The bacteria were pelleted by centrifugation at 15,000 × g, 60 min, 4°C. Then, the supernatant was loaded onto a Ni2+-NTA column and washed with 30 ml of wash buffer (500 mM NaCl, 20 mM Na2HPO4, 50 mM Tris, 25 mM imidazole, pH 7.4). Finally, the protein was eluted by elution buffer (500 mM NaCl, 20 mM Na2HPO4, 50 mM Tris, 500 mM imidazole, pH 7.4). The purity of the eluted protein (VHH) was evaluated by SDS-PAGE.

### Evaluation of the ability of anti-HER2 VHHs to recognize HER2+ cells by using flow cytometry

BT474, SKOV-3, and MDA-MB-231 were purchased from American Type Culture Collection (ATCC, VA, USA). OVASC-1, an ascites-derived epithelial ovarian cancer cells, was obtained from a patient with advanced metastatic disease . Hybri-Care (ATCC, VA, USA), McCoy’s 5A (Gibco, NY, USA), Leibovitz’s L-15 (ATCC, VA, USA) medium, all supplemented with 10% FBS and 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin (10,000 U/ml) (Gibco, NY, USA), were used for BT474, SKOV-3, and MDA-MB-23, respectively. OVASC-1 was cultured in RPMI-1640 (Sigma-Aldrich, MA, USA) supplemented with 15% FBS, 1% Penicillin-Streptomycin (10,000 U/ml), and 2.5 μg/ml insulin (Sigma-Aldrich, MA, USA). The expressed VHHs were then incubated with HER2+ (BT474 and SKOV-3) and HER2¯ (MDA-MB-231 and OVASC-1) cancer cell lines. Approximately 106 cells were counted and washed using DPBS-1% FBS. Then, equivalent to 100 nM binding sites of trastuzumab (Trazimera®, Pfizer), pertuzumab (Perjeta®, Genentech) or VHHs were added to the cells and incubated on ice for 60 min. After washing the cells, FITC-conjugated anti-Human IgG (Abcam, MA, USA) was used as isotype control for trastuzumab and pertuzumab, whereas secondary anti-Histag antibody (Abcam, MA, USA) was used as isotype control for VHHs. Cells were washed three times and then analyzed using Beckman-Coulter Gallios flow cytometer at Rutgers Flow cytometry core facility.

### Evaluation of the toxicity of the anti-HER2 VHHs

The toxicity of anti-HER2 VHHs, trastuzumab (Trazimera®, Pfizer), and pertuzumab (Perjeta®, Genentech), were evaluated using BT-474 and SKOV-3 cancer cells. Briefly, 10 × 106 cells were seeded in a 96-well plate. The next day, cells were treated with 1333.3, 13.3, 13, 0.13, 0.013 and 0 nM of VHH or antibody. After 72 h, the media was removed, and 100 μl of fresh media supplemented with 10% WST-1 reagent (Abcam, MA, USA) was added. After 4 h, the plate was read at 440 nm and 600 nm as a reference wavelength. All experiments were performed in triplicates and data are presented as mean ± s.d. (standard deviation).

### Measurement of VHH binding affinity and kinetics using Biolayer Interferometer

To evaluate the binding affinity (KD) and constant rates of association (Kon) and dissociation (Koff) of VHHs, an Octet RED96e instrument (Sartorius) Biolayer Interferometer (BLI) along with an Octet® Streptavidin (SA) (Sartorius, PA, USA) Biosensor were used. After soaking the sensor for at least 10 min in DPBS + 0.1% Casein, biotinylated HER2 was loaded onto the Streptavidin (SA) Biosensor until 1 nm shift was reached. Next, the sensor was dipped into the washing buffer (DPBS + 0.05% Tween 20 + 0.1% Casein) for 2 min to reach the baseline. Then, sensor was submerged into wells containing 60, 30, 15, 7.5, 3.75, 1.875, and 0 nM of purified anti-HER2 VHH for 5 min (association step). In dissociation step, wells were dipped into washing buffer (DPBS + 0.05% Tween 20 + 0.1% Casein) for 10 min to acquire data (Supplementary Table 3). The data were then analyzed using Octet Data Analysis HT 11.1 software. For data analysis, the sensograms were subtracted from the reference, and fitted into 1:1 binding model. Finally, the affinity and kinetics were analyzed using “Association and Dissociation”. All BLI data acquisition and analysis studies were performed at Biophysics Core Facility in the Department of Chemistry at Princeton University.

### In-silico modeling and docking of anti-HER2 VHH

The complementarity-determining regions (CDRs) of A1 and E5 anti-HER2 VHHs were outlined using ImmunoGenetics (IMGT)/V-Quest database . The 3D structure was predicted via the ChimeraX software (Version 1.5) using the alpha fold algorithm . The best 3D model was further refined using the GalaxyRefine (http://galaxy.seoklab.org/cgi-bin/submit.cgi?type=REFINE) to relieve errors that might have occurred in the prediction process . Next, the quality of the refined tertiary structures was corroborated by Ramachandran plot analysis using PROCHECK (SAVES) (https://saves.mbi.ucla.edu/).

The crystalized structure of HER2 was obtained from the RCSB Protein Data Bank under the accession number 3BE1. The ClusPro server (https://cluspro.bu.edu/home.php) was used to carry out the docking process between the VHHs and HER2 ectodomain . To visualize and analyze the docking, the PyMOL Molecular Graphics System, Version 2.5.4 Schrödinger, LLC was utilized .

### Antibody-dependent cell mediated cytotoxicity

Using a previously published method, we generated a bispecific killer cell engager (BiKE) by fusing E5 anti-HER2 VHH with an anti-CD16a VHH . For simplicity, this BiKE molecule will be referred to as BiKE-E5:C1. Then, the ability of BiKE-E5:C1 to induce antibody-dependent cell mediated cytotoxicity (ADCC) was evaluated and compared with mAbs trastuzumab and pertuzumab as described previously . In brief, target cancer cells (i.e., SKOV-3 cells) were seeded at the density of 1×104 cancer cells per well in a tissue culture treated 96-well plate. The next day, BiKE-E5:C1 (10 pM), trastuzumab (10 pM), pertuzumab (10 pM), trastuzumab plus pertuzumab (10 pM + 10 pM), or BiKE-E5:C1 plus pertuzumab (10 pM + 10 pM) were added to the cells and incubated at 37°C for 30 min. Next, CD16+ low affinity NK92 cells (ATCC, Manassas, VA) were added as effector cells to target cells to make E:T ratios of 0 and 2 followed by incubation for 6 h at 37°C. Next, each well was washed twice using DPBS to remove NK92 cells. Finally, 10% alamarBlue™ HS Cell Viability Reagent was added to the plate and read using a Tecan Infinite M Plex plate reader.

### Evaluation of the application of anti-HER2 VHH in cell imaging

The internalization of A1 and E5 VHHs after binding to HER2 receptor in SKOV-3 cancer cells were examined using confocal microscopy. SKOV-3 cells were seeded at the density of 2.5 × 104 cells on a Nunc Lab-Tek™ chamber slide (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA). The next day, cells were treated with 20 nM of VHH and incubated on ice for 60 min. Next, the antibody solution was discarded, and all wells were washed three times using ice-cold DPBS. To examine the rate of internalization at different time points, RPMI media supplemented with 5% FBS was added to the to the wells and incubated at 37°C for 1, 2, and 4 h, followed by washing and fixation. The cells were fixed by 3.7% paraformaldehyde for 15 min at 37°C, followed by three steps of washing. Afterwards, cells were permeabilized using 0.1% Triton X100 for 15 min at RT. Cells were incubated with blocking buffer (DPBS with 2% BSA) for 2 h at RT. Next, secondary antibody, FITC labeled anti-HisTag (Abcam, MA, USA), was added and incubated at RT for 1 h. After three steps of washing, cells were stained with 300 nM DAPI for 3 min followed by three times wash. Finally, HER2 internalization was observed under a Leica TCS SP8 Confocal Microscope (Leica Microsystems GmbH) with the 63× objective lens using immersion oil. Z-stack images were taken each at 500 nm apart. The images of different z-stacks were processed by Leica software.

### Evaluation of the application of anti-HER2 VHH in immunohistochemistry

Female immune-compromised NCG mice (Charles River) were injected subcutaneously with 5 × 106 of SKOV-3 (HER2+) and MDA-MB-231 (HER2¯) cells to form tumors at their dorsal flanks. When tumor sizes reached ~500 mm3, mice were euthanized, tumors removed and washed with saline, placed inside a Cryomold filled with Tissue-Plus™ O.C.T compound (Thermo Fisher Scientific, MA, USA), and then snap frozen on dry ice. Cryosectioning was performed at the Rutgers Research Pathology Services core facility. Next, the sections were stained with anti-HER2 E5 and A1 VHHs, followed by anti-Histag secondary antibody. A commercially available anti-HER2 antibody, EPR19547–12 (Abcam, MA, USA), suitable for immunohistochemistry (IHC) was used as the positive control. Photomicrography was conducted using a Leica microscope (2× objective).

## Results

### Expression of HER2 and immunization of llama

Using standard genetic engineering techniques, the HER2 antigen was expressed in HEK293F cells and purified. The SDS-PAGE results estimated the purity of the purified HER2 to be approximately 95% (Figure 1A). While the theoretical molecular weight of the HER2 (without secretory signal) is 72,633 Da, the migration of the protein is close to the 100 kDa marker. This indicates that the expressed HER2 went through post-translational modification such as glycosylation . The purified HER2 was then used to immunize a llama using the protocol shown in Figure 1B. ELISA assay performed on blood, drawn approximately seven weeks post immunization, showed significant elevation in anti-HER2 IgG levels (OD450 of 1.5 after 1/20,000 dilution), which indicates the potent immune response to the injected HER2 antigen (Figure 1C). On day 75 post immunization of llama, blood was drawn, PBMCs isolated, a cDNA and phagemid library were generated followed by phage display (Figure 1D–1F). Then, several colonies were selected and examined for specificity/selectivity. The results of ELISA showed that the selected anti-HER2 VHHs were specific to the HER2 antigen and had negligible interaction with HER1, HER3, HER4, BSA, or skim milk (Figure 1G).

### Evaluation of the ability of Anti-HER2 VHHs to bind to HER2 antigen in plates using ELISA

Several anti-HER2 VHH clones were sequenced, analyzed, and grouped based on the phylogenic tree. One sequence from each group with the highest affinity and specificity to HER2 was selected (Figure 2A). Each sequence was designed to have a c-Myc (GSEQKLISEEDL) and Histag (HHHHHHHHHHHH) at its C-terminal. The nine selected anti-HER2 VHHs were then expressed in E. coli and purified. The yield of expression for all VHHs (except clones A3 and C9) was between 3–5 mg/l and with an estimated purity of above 95% (Figure 2B). Clones A3 and C9 were removed from the subsequent studies due to their low solubility leading to aggregation and low yield. To evaluate the application of the purified anti-HER2 VHHs in ELISA, an ELISA plate was coated with HER2 antigen. The results of the ELISA experiment showed all seven anti-HER2 VHHs could effectively bind to HER2 antigen without cross reactivity with BSA (Figure 2C).

### Evaluation of the ability of anti-HER2 VHHs to bind to HER2 antigen using flow cytometry

In the next step, we evaluated the ability of the anti-HER2 VHHs to bind to HER2 antigen on the surface of HER2+ cancer cells. For this purpose, the equimolar of binding sites of purified anti-HER2 VHHs and commercial anti-HER2 monoclonal antibodies (trastuzumab and pertuzumab) were used to measure the HER2 expression on the surface of BT474 and SKOV-3 (HER2+) cancer cells. MDA-MB-231 and OVASC-1 (HER2¯) cancer cells were used as negative controls. The flow cytometry data showed that the selected VHHs could recognize HER2 on the surface of HER2+ cancer cells with negligible binding to HER2¯ cancer cells (Figure 3A–B). Analysis of the total mean fluorescent intensity (MFI) of cells showed that the cells labeled with trastuzumab and pertuzumab had higher MFI than anti-HER2 VHHs (Table 1).

### Evaluation of the cytotoxicity of the anti-HER2 VHHs

To determine whether the selected anti-HER2 VHHs induce toxicity to HER2+ cells, a cell toxicity assay was performed using BT474 and SKOV-3 cancer cells. Trastuzumab and pertuzumab were used as controls. The results of this experiment revealed that the VHHs, similar to trastuzumab and pertuzumab, did not induce statistically significant toxicity to SKOV-3 HER2+ cancer cells at concentration as high as 133 nM (Figure 4A). However, BT474 cells appeared to be slightly sensitive to E5 and E9 VHHs with approximately 5% drop in viability (*t-test, p<0.05) (Figure 4B). While pertuzumab showed no toxicity to BT474, trastuzumab showed significant toxicity at concentrations higher than 13 nM (Figure 4B).

### Measurement of the binding affinity of anti-HER2 VHHs using biolayer interferometer (BLI)

Based on the data shown so far, we selected E5 and A1 clones as our top candidates and used BLI to measure their affinities towards HER2 antigen. The BLI data showed that the affinities of A1 and E5 clones toward HER2 were 1.3 and 0.72 nM, respectively (Figure 5A–B). Then, we performed epitope mapping to examine whether the E5 anti-HER2 VHH binds to the same epitope on HER2 antigen as trastuzumab and pertuzumab. The BLI results revealed the followings: 1) when the E5 VHH bound to HER2 antigen first, it interfered with the binding kinetics of trastuzumab but did not block it (Figures 5C–5E); 2) when trastuzumab bound to HER2 antigen first, it completely blocked the binding of E5 VHH (Figures 5F); 3) the E5 VHH had no interference with pertuzumab binding to HER2 antigen (Figure 5G–5I); 4) the epitope mapping results also showed that the binding sites of E5 and A1 on HER2 antigen are shared as the binding of A1 VHH to HER2 antigen was blocked by E5 VHH (Figure 5J).

### In-silico VHH modeling and docking

Following the BLI data, we used the AlphaFold 2 algorithm to model the tertiary structures of E5 and A1 anti-HER2 VHHs and visualize their binding sites on HER2 antigen. The AlphaFold is a high-precision software that uses artificial intelligence algorithms to model the protein structures . The predicted structures for E5 and A1 VHHs show that both antibodies were composed of nine anti-parallel β-sheets, which is the hallmark of immunoglobulin structure (Figure 6A–B). The function of the disulfide bonds (C-C) between frameworks 1 and 3 (shown in orange color) is to stabilize the elongated CDR3 structure . The Ramachandran analysis of the E5 and A1 modeling also revealed that >94% of the amino acid residues were in most favored region and <6% in the allowed region with the ERRAT score of 100%, indicating no error was found in the modeled residues. As shown in Figure 6C, E5 and A1 VHHs share significant structural similarities; however, a noticeable structural difference in the loop region can be observed. This structural disparity likely contributed to the differences in their binding affinities. However, the Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) of the aligned structures was calculated to be 0.367, indicating a high degree of structural similarity between the compared protein structures. This suggests a close alignment and supports the notion that despite the observed difference, they share substantial overall structural characteristics. Using this information, we examined antibody-antigen docking and the results showed that both VHHs bind to domain IV of HER2 ectodomain, which is in agreement with the BLI epitope mapping data. Domain IV of HER2 is located adjacent to the transmembrane domain, which stabilizes the interaction between HER2 and other HER members, such as HER1 and HER3 .

### Evaluation of the application of anti-HER2 VHH in BiKE engineering and cancer therapy

Consistent with our molecular modeling results, others have also shown that trastuzumab binds to domain IV of HER2 antigen , whereas pertuzumab has been shown to bind to domain II (Figure 7A). We have previously reported that the E5 VHH can be used to engineer a BiKE molecule (BiKE-E5:C1) with ability to activate NK cells and kill HER2+ cancer cells more effectively than trastuzumab . Since trastuzumab plus pertuzumab is currently available in the clinic under the brand name PHESGO® for cancer therapy, we examined whether the engineered BiKE-E5:C1 plus pertuzumab can kill HER2+ cancer cells more effectively than PHESGO®. Here, we combined BiKE-E5:C1 with pertuzumab instead of trastuzumab because the BLI and molecular modeling data showed E5 VHH competes with trastuzumab but not pertuzumab. The results of ADCC assay demonstrated that the engineered BiKE-E5:C1 could kill SKOV-3 cancer cells more efficiently than trastuzumab, and the combination of BiKE-E5:C1 with pertuzumab provided an advantage over the trastzumab plus pertuzumab (Figure 7B).

### Evaluation of the application of the anti-HER2 VHHs in cell imaging

Since the selected E5 and A1 anti-HER2 VHHs showed high affinity and no toxicity to cells, we evaluated their application as a reagent for cell imaging. For this purpose, SKOV-3 cells were seeded, then the binding and internalization of the VHHs into the cells were studied over time by a confocal microscope. The results of this experiment showed that both A1 and E5 clones internalized into SKOV-3 cells as early as 1 hour and the internalization process was completed in 3 to 5 h (Figure 8). Prior literature showed that trastuzumab binds and internalizes into HER2+ cancer cells in less than 4 h .

### Evaluation of the application of the VHHs in immunohistochemistry

To examine the ability of the E5 and A1 VHHs to differentiate HER2+ from HER2⁻ tumor tissues with potential application in immunohistochemistry and ex-vivo cancer phenotyping, SKOV-3 (HER2+) and MDA-MB-231 (HER2¯) tissue sections were prepared and stained with A1 and E5 VHHs. A commercially available anti-HER2 mAb against HER2 was used as the positive control. The results of this experiment illustrated that both E5 and A1 anti-HER2 VHHs stained the HER2+ tissue without cross-reactivity with HER2¯ tissue (Figure 9). These results also validated the specificity of E5 and A1 VHHs by binding to HER2+ antigens without cross-reactivity with other antigens in tissue slices.

## Discussion

HER2 is a receptor that is frequently overexpressed on a variety of solid tumors and their metastatic lesions, making it a suitable target for preclinical and clinical studies. To generate single-domain antibodies against the HER2 antigen, we expressed the HER2 protein in mammalian cells and used it to immunize a llama. Once the llama’s immune response against the HER2 antigen was confirmed by ELISA, were isolated anti-HER2 VHHs from the PBMCs (Figure 1). To make the isolated anti-HER2 VHHs suitable for use as a reagent for HER2 detection, we included a Histag and c-Myc tag at the C-terminals of the constructs. Using the tagged anti-HER2 VHHs, we observed that they effectively bind to the HER2 antigen in coated plates and on the surface of the HER2+ cancer cells (Figures 2 and 3). These results demonstrate the application of the isolated VHHs in both ELISA and flow cytometry. It is noteworthy that the flow cytometry data show the MFI generated by the VHHs in HER2+ cancer cells was slightly lower than that of trastuzumab and pertuzumab. One reason for this difference is that the secondary antibody used to detect trastuzumab and pertuzumab was polyclonal against the light and heavy chains of the antibody (1 antibody/ multiple labels), resulting in a significant boost in signal (Table 1). In contrast, the secondary antibody used in our experiment to detect Histag in anti-HER2 VHHs was monoclonal (1 VHH/ 1 label) which generated slightly lower signal intensity. This difference in MFI can be overcome by using a polyclonal secondary antibody against Histag. The second reason is that IgG-based antibodies are bivalent, leading to higher avidity compared to VHHs, which are monovalent. Nevertheless, the flow cytometry data show that the selected anti-HER2 VHHs can differentiate between HER2+ and HER2¯ cells and can be used as a suitable reagent for cell phenotyping by flow cytometry. In Figure 3 and Table 1, it can be observed that trastuzumab, pertuzumab, and anti-HER2 VHHs exhibit some binding (although minor) to HER2¯ cancer cells. The reason is that all cells of epithelial origin (both cancerous and normal) express HER2, including HER2¯ cancer cells. In immunochemistry analysis, tumor cells are scored as 0, 1+, 2+, and 3+. Scores of 0 and 1+ are considered HER2¯, even though HER2 is present. A score of 2+ is considered equivocal, and a score of 3+ is indicative of HER2+ status. That explains why trastuzumab shows low level binding to MDA-MB-231 cells, which is a HER2¯ breast cancer cell line of epithelial origin. Scoring a cell line as HER2¯ means it is not suitable for HER2 immunotherapy, even though it expresses HER2.

In the next step, we performed a cell toxicity assay to examine the potential application of the anti-HER2 VHHs in cancer imaging. The cell toxicity data showed that the isolated VHHs did not induce significant toxicity to cancer cells suggesting the potential application of the E5 and A1 clones for in vivo cancer imaging (Figure 4) . Furthermore, we determined the affinity of the E5 and A1 VHH clones toward the HER2 antigen. The BLI data revealed that both clones exhibited high affinity (Figure 5A–5B). Using BLI, we then investigated whether E5 anti-HER2 VHH shared an epitope with trastuzumab or pertuzumab. The BLI sensograms revealed that the E5 VHH shared the same epitope as trastuzumab, although it appeared to be targeting a hidden site that was not fully accessible to trastuzumab (Figure 5E–5F). In contrast, the E5 VHH did not compete with pertuzumab binding (Figure 5G–5H). To model these findings, we performed in-silico modeling and docking, and the results showed that indeed both E5 and A1 VHHs bind to domain IV of HER2 antigen (Figure 6). The E5 and A1 VHHs also showed a high degree of structural similarity, suggesting that they are most likely the result of in vivo maturation of the same B cell clone. Considering that the E5 VHH targeted the same epitope as trastuzumab but a different epitope than pertuzumab, we investigated its potential use in creating a BiKE to kill HER2+ cancer cells. To examine this possibility, we used the E5 VHH to engineer a BiKE and evaluated its ability to augment the cancer killing efficiency of pertuzumab. The ADCC assay results showed that BiKE plus pertuzumab killed cancer cells more effectively than BiKE alone or trastuzumab plus pertuzumab (Figure 7), suggesting that it could potentially be used as a replacement for trastuzumab. Our cell imaging and immunohistochemistry data also demonstrated that the top two performing VHHs (E5 and A1) could effectively differentiate HER2+ from HER2¯ cells individually or in tissues, indicating their potential use as diagnostic agents (Figures 8 and 9). This capabilities could be attributed to their high affinity, specificity, and selectivity. Moreover, the high affinity and specificity of the E5 and A1 VHHs in combination with their non-toxic nature raises the possibility of using these two antibodies as agents for in vivo cancer phenotyping in patients.

## Conclusions

In the past, anti-HER2 VHHs that do not target the same epitope as trastuzumab have been utilized in applications such as ELISA, flow cytometry, and tumor imaging . In this study, we report the sequences of single-domain antibodies with high affinity and specificity toward the HER2 antigen, targeting the same epitope as trastuzumab, and demonstrate their application in ELISA, flow cytometry, cell imaging, BiKE engineering, cancer cell killing, and immunohistochemistry. Therefore, the reported VHHs add to the repertoire of anti-HER2 antibodies that can potentially be used as diagnostic reagents or therapeutic antibodies. Considering that the discovered VHHs are stable, soluble, and can be produced in large quantities in E. coli, they provide a low-cost alternative to mAbs that are mainly generated and produced in mammalian cells.
